root.name: Van Geet Opening: Sicilian Two Knights
root.moves: 1. Nc3 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4

parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.

root.name: Ruy Lopez: Vinogradov Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 Qe7

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.

parent.name: Alekhine Defense
parent.overview: Black attacks e4 at once with 1...Nf6 and, after 2.e5 Nd5, invites White to build a broad centre with c4, d4 and perhaps f4, planning to attack that centre later with ...d6, ...Nb6, ...Bg4, ...c5 and ...dxe5. White's job is to keep or use the extra space, either with the most ambitious Four Pawns Attack (4.c4 Nb6 5.f4), the popular Modern Variation 4.Nf3, or the less forcing Exchange 5.exd6; 2.Nc3 avoids the main line entirely. Positions lose symmetry from the start and are unbalanced, with a space edge for White against Black's counterplay on the overextended pawns. The opening is regarded as sound, original and tricky but risky (moderate to high), and is only moderately common at the top: Fischer, Korchnoi, Ivanchuk and occasionally Carlsen have played it.

root.name: Sicilian Defense: Myers Attack, with a4

subtree_most_played.name: Sicilian Defense: Myers Attack, with h4

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

subtree_most_played.moves: 1. e4 g6 2. d4 Bg7 3. Nc3 d5

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Modern Defense
parent.overview: Against 1.d4 Black plays 1...g6, fianchettoing the king's bishop (...Bg7) and delaying the knight on f6 and any central commitment. The idea is hypermodern: let White build a pawn centre, then attack it from the flanks with ...d6 and ...c5 or ...e5, with queenside play (...b5, ...a5) backed by the Bg7. Because ...Nf6 is delayed it can still become a King's Indian (after c4 and Nc3), a Pirc (after e4) or a Grünfeld, or stay a separate Modern. White's common set-ups are a classical centre (c4, e4, Nc3, Be3), the Averbakh with c4, or the pseudo-Austrian or Samisch-like f4/f3 centres with a kingside space attack. Sources disagree on the character: the line is balanced and sound but can become very sharp and awkward for Black if the kingside weakens.
